notes.meaning: King Nebuchadnezzar brought his entire army to besiege Jerusalem during the winter of Zedekiah's ninth year. A siege meant surrounding the city and cutting off all food and supplies until the people surrendered. This began the terrible eighteen-month ordeal that Jeremiah had repeatedly warned would come.

The Babylonian army finally battered down the city walls in Zedekiah's eleventh year. The people inside had run out of food and were too weak from famine to fight back any longer. God's warnings through Jeremiah proved true, while the false prophets who promised peace were proven completely wrong.

Babylonian commanders marched inside and set up their seats at the Middle Gate to take military control. Sitting in the city gate was an ancient sign of judging and ruling the city. Heathen generals bearing names of pagan idols now ruled the very spot where Judah's leaders had once governed.

When King Zedekiah and his soldiers saw that the enemy had broken in, they fled in secret during the night. They slipped out through a gate near the royal garden and headed down toward the Jordan valley. Zedekiah abandoned his people to save himself, vainly attempting to run from God's appointed judgment.

The Babylonian soldiers chased the fleeing king and captured him near Jericho before he could cross the Jordan River. They hauled him north to Riblah, where Nebuchadnezzar put him on trial like an ordinary rebel. Zedekiah had broken his oath of allegiance, and he could not escape the hand of God.

At Riblah, Nebuchadnezzar forced Zedekiah to watch his own young sons being executed. The king of Babylon also executed all the leading nobles of Judah. This brutal act ended the royal line on the throne and judged the rulers who had hardened their hearts against God.

Nebuchadnezzar then put out Zedekiah's eyes and bound him in bronze chains to be dragged off to Babylon. This exact event fulfilled two prophecies: Zedekiah saw the Babylonian king face to face, yet he never saw Babylon itself because he entered it blind. The king who had shut his eyes to God's truth spent the rest of his days in darkness.

The Babylonians set fire to the royal palace and to the homes of the common people. They also tore down the protective walls surrounding Jerusalem so the city could no longer defend itself. Because the nation clung to sin, God withdrew His protection and let the city be leveled.

Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, gathered the survivors left in the city along with those who had previously surrendered. He marched them away as captives on the long journey to Babylon. These people were driven into exile away from the pleasant homeland they had taken for granted.

The Babylonians left behind only the poorest people in Judah, who had owned no property of their own. Nebuzaradan gave them the vineyards and fields that used to belong to the wealthy rulers. In God's justice, the humble poor were blessed with land, while the proud who had mistreated them were carried off empty-handed.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that giving land to the poorest residents was a practical political move designed to win their loyalty and attach them to their new Babylonian rulers.

notes.meaning: King Nebuchadnezzar issued specific instructions to Nebuzaradan regarding the safety of Jeremiah. The Babylonian king had likely heard about the prophet from deserters or through earlier captives taken with Jeconiah. God worked behind the scenes through a pagan emperor to watch over His faithful messenger.

Nebuchadnezzar ordered his commander to protect Jeremiah, keep him from all harm, and grant whatever he requested. Even in the middle of a violent military conquest, God shielded Jeremiah from danger. While the persecutors faced judgment, the Lord faithfully fulfilled His promise to rescue the prophet.

Nebuzaradan and the highest commanders in the Babylonian army carried out the king's royal decree. These foreign officers personally saw to it that the prophet was located and cared for. God arranged for the most powerful commanders in the conquering army to become Jeremiah's protectors.

The officers brought Jeremiah out of the prison courtyard and placed him with Gedaliah, who took him home. Gedaliah came from a family that had previously protected Jeremiah, and he gave the prophet a safe place to stay. Jeremiah was now free to walk about and live quietly among the remaining people of Judah.

This message had come to Jeremiah earlier, while he was still locked up in the courtyard of the guard. The account looks back in time to show that God had not forgotten the Ethiopian official who had rescued Jeremiah from the muddy cistern. God always remembers and rewards those who show kindness to His servants.

God directed Jeremiah to give a personal word of comfort to Ebed-melech the Cushite. The Lord announced that His warnings of destruction against Jerusalem would happen right before Ebed-melech's eyes. Even though terrible ruin was coming upon the city, God wanted this foreigner to know that everything remained under divine control.

The Lord assured Ebed-melech that he would be delivered on the day Jerusalem fell. He would not be handed over to the royal officials whose revenge he feared after rescuing Jeremiah. God saw his inner dread and provided him with personal comfort to calm his fears.

God promised to rescue Ebed-melech from the sword and grant him his life as his prize. This protection was given because Ebed-melech had placed his trust in the Lord rather than being paralyzed by fear of men. His brave rescue of Jeremiah was the living fruit of his faith, and God faithfully kept him safe.
